quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

Pennsylvania civil death registration began in 1906, so this 1908 death has a state certificate. The 1860 census (S2) is already cited in the project tree relationship R1, but no assertions have been extracted from it for this parentage question. Patrick would be ~15 and Thomas ~42 in 1860. If they appear in the same household, this corroborates the father-son relationship and reveals Patrick's mother (and any siblings). The 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly, but shared surname and household position are indirect co-residency evidence. The United States Census, 1860 collection is name-searchable. Search Flynn and Flinn spellings.

By 1870 Patrick would be ~25 and Thomas ~52. The 1870 census bridges the gap between 1860 and 1880 and may show Patrick still in Thomas's household, or Thomas in Patrick's. Patrick's mother may also appear if still living. The United States Census, 1870 collection is name-searchable. Search Flynn and Flinn spellings. An Ancestry 1870 census collection is also stored in external collections (ancestry:7163) if the FamilySearch search yields no result.

The 1880 census is the FIRST U.S. census to record explicit relationships to the head of household. If Patrick (~35) appears in Thomas's household as 'son,' or Thomas (~62) appears in Patrick's as 'father,' this is stronger relationship evidence than any earlier census. The 1880 census also records each person's parents' birthplaces, confirming the Irish origin. The United States Census, 1880 collection is name-searchable. Search Flynn and Flinn spellings.

Patrick would be ~55 in 1900 and died in 1908. The 1900 census states explicit relationships to the head of household and asks for parents' countries of birth. Thomas (born ~1818) would be ~82 and may still be alive. Any listing of Patrick in 1900 would confirm parents' birthplaces and may show Thomas in the household. The United States Census, 1900 collection is name-searchable.

REQUIRED PARENTAGE ITEM — dedicated search for the marriage of Thomas Flynn to Patrick's unknown mother. Thomas and Patrick's mother likely married in Ireland before Patrick's birth (~1845), but Thomas may have remarried in Pennsylvania. The Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records collection (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) is name-searchable (personCount 982415), covering 1708-1985, and should be searched for any Thomas Flynn marriage entry. The marriage record supplies the mother's maiden name, confirms them as a married couple, and by its date relative to Patrick's birth corroborates Thomas as father otherwise known only from the indirect 1850 census co-residence. Note: the marriage alone does not prove Patrick is their child; that link still requires a record placing Patrick with the parents.

Roman Catholic parishes in Schuylkill County were under the Diocese of Philadelphia (archdiocese from 1875); the Diocese of Scranton (erected 1868) took the northern counties, not Schuylkill (loc_001). If Patrick's younger siblings were baptized in a Pennsylvania parish after the family's arrival (~1847-1870), those baptism records name Thomas as father and his wife as mother — direct parentage evidence. Patrick's own confirmation record (if held in Schuylkill County) would also name his parents. items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

items.question: Besides Mary, John, Rebecca, William and Joseph, who were the other children of Thomas Hale (b. about 1810, Pennsylvania; d. 1868, Greene County, Ohio) and his wife Sarah?
items.rationale: Primary research objective. The tree holds the couple and five children; no records have been searched yet for any others.

entry.rationale: The 1840 census records household members as tally marks by sex and age bracket, not by name, but it reveals any children born before Mary (~1836) — an older child not yet in the tree — as well as the total count of children present in 1840. Thomas (about 30) should appear as head; Mary and John, if already born, would fall in the under-5 and 5-10 brackets. Any child in an older bracket signals a sibling older than Mary. The collections_search service was unavailable this session; availability planned from the locality guide (loc_001) and the well-established US Census series. Consider spelling variants Hail and Haile.

The 1850 census names every household member with age and birthplace — the first census to do so. Thomas's household should contain the five known children (Mary ~14, John ~12, Rebecca ~9, William ~6, Joseph ~3) plus any additional children born between 1847 and 1850 or any older child born before 1836 not yet in the tree. The locality guide (loc_001) lists this as United States Census, 1850 (collection 1401638); personCount could not be verified this session due to a service outage. Also check adjacent households in the same Greene County township for Hale-surnamed neighbors, who may be adult children who established their own households but remained close by. Ancestry carries the same census and may index spelling variants differently.

By 1860 the oldest known children would be approaching or past the age of leaving home (Mary ~24, John ~22); any children born after Joseph (~1847) would still be in the household. This census is the primary way to identify children born between 1848 and 1860 who would not yet appear in the 1850 household. The locality guide (loc_001) lists this as United States Census, 1860 (collection 1473181); personCount could not be verified this session. Also search adjacent Hale-surnamed households for adult children who moved out but remained nearby. Consider spelling variants.

Thomas died in 1868. In the 1870 census Sarah appears as widowed head or living with an adult child. Any children still in the household (likely those born after 1847) would be named. This census also captures the family structure two years after Thomas's death and can confirm which children survived to that date. The locality guide (loc_001) lists this as United States Census, 1870 (collection 1438024); personCount could not be verified this session. Also search adjacent Hale-surnamed households for adult children. This census (FAN angle): a Hale household nearby with the same age-range adults as Sarah's children may identify a child not found in earlier enumerations.

Thomas Hale died in 1868 in Greene County. His will, if any, would name his children as beneficiaries; an intestate proceeding would produce a heirs petition or distribution record listing all children entitled to a share of the estate. This is the single record type most likely to enumerate all of Thomas's children in one document. The locality guide (loc_001) lists Ohio Probate Records, 1789-1996 (collection 1992421); its quirks note the Greene County Probate Court dates from 1852, so an 1868 filing sits in that court. The date range runs to 1878 to allow for a prolonged estate settlement. PersonCount could not be verified this session.

If any Hale child was under 18 at Thomas's death in 1868, the Greene County Probate Court would have recorded a guardian appointment, directly naming the minor child or children. Joseph, the youngest known child (born ~1847), would have been about 21 in 1868 — barely of age. Any child born after 1850 would have been a minor requiring a guardian. The date range upper bound of 1886 reflects the latest year a child born in 1868 would turn 18. This item targets the same collection as item 5 (Ohio Probate Records, 1789-1996) but specifically searches guardianship filings, not estate or will records; searching both is warranted. The bounds on the date range are set by when such a child would turn 18.

Marriage records for Thomas and Sarah's children name the bride or groom, the father (or family head), and sometimes both parents. Daughters who married changed surname and disappear from 'Hale' searches in every other record type unless caught here; this search specifically covers brides surnamed Hale as well as grooms. A daughter found marrying in Greene County but not yet in the tree reveals an additional child. The locality guide (loc_001) lists Ohio County Marriages, 1789-2016 (collection 1614804). The date range covers when children born roughly 1832–1860 would typically marry (ages ~18–35). PersonCount could not be verified this session. Consider spelling variants Hail and Haile.

Ohio civil birth registration did not begin until 1867 and was poorly observed for decades. Children of Thomas and Sarah born in the 1830s through 1860s would appear in church baptism or christening records, not civil records. FamilySearch holds various Greene County church collections; Quaker, Methodist, and Presbyterian congregations were active in the area during this period. A baptism or membership record naming Thomas and Sarah as parents could reveal a child not found in any census. If FamilySearch records are browse-only (personCount 0), images should be browsed for the relevant years. Local Greene County church archives and the Ohio History Connection may hold records not yet digitized.

A family burial plot in a Greene County cemetery may list all of Thomas and Sarah's children on headstones, including children who died in infancy or childhood and would not appear in census records. FamilySearch holds some Ohio cemetery transcriptions; FindAGrave (Ancestry) has widespread Greene County coverage and groups family members by burial location. Ohio civil death registration began in 1867 but was incomplete initially: children who died before 1867 appear only in cemetery, church, or family records. For children who died after 1867, Ohio death certificates (held at the Ohio History Connection and partially on FamilySearch) name the deceased and sometimes the parents. The date range of 1830-1920 covers both early infant deaths and later deaths of surviving adult children who outlived Thomas and Sarah.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

The FamilySearch 'Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994' (collection 1999196) covers this period but is browse-only (personCount 0) — this is an image browse of Schuylkill County's will books and administration dockets, not a name search. The FamilySearch 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records' (collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, name-searchable) covers 1708-1985 and is the first access point. If found, this record confirms Thomas and his wife as a couple and supplies the mother's maiden name, which is unavailable from either census or the 1908 death certificate. By its date relative to Patrick's 1845 birth, it also corroborates a father otherwise named only by indirect census evidence and a secondary-informant death certificate. Note the limit: the marriage record alone does not prove Patrick is their child — a record placing Patrick with the parents is still needed to close the parentage.

Search the name-searchable FamilySearch 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records' (collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) under Thomas Flynn's name for baptism entries of his children other than Patrick. Some Pennsylvania Catholic marriage records of this era name the groom's parents; the marriage witnesses are often siblings or close relatives of the groom. quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

A will or administration record naming Patrick as a son would be direct parentage evidence and would likely name Thomas's wife, closing the maternal parentage gap the 1908 death certificate left open (the informant, son-in-law James Brown, listed only 'Thomas Flynn' as father). The Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683-1994 collection is browse-only (personCount 0); image group 007936749 (Schuylkill County probate records, 1851-1930) covers the same material and is likewise browse-only (personCount 0). loc_001 confirms probate records are held by the county Register of Wills and available from 1811. Thomas Flynn's plausible lifespan (born ~1818) sets the date window: he could have died anywhere from the early 1850s through the 1890s, well past the question's window.

FAN item — Thomas Flynn's household. The 1880 census introduced the first explicit 'relationship to head' column in US federal census history. Searching for Thomas Flynn (~62 in 1880) in Schuylkill County would reveal any children remaining in his household with their relationship stated explicitly as 'son' or 'daughter.' Also search for Patrick Flynn (~35 in 1880), who by then likely had his own household: children named after grandparents would reinforce the Thomas parentage by naming convention. The United States Census, 1880 is name-searchable. This census also falls in the documented high-severity timeline gap (1860-1908).

FAN item — Thomas Flynn's household. The 1870 census is an identified gap in the proof summary. Thomas would be ~52 and Patrick ~25; Patrick may still be in Thomas's household, which would add a third consecutive census co-residence to the two already established (1850 and 1860). More importantly, Thomas's full 1870 household composition would name any siblings who had not yet left home and, critically, Thomas's wife — whose name has not yet appeared in any searched record and whose identity is a core part of the parentage question ('Who were the PARENTS'). The United States Census, 1870 is name-searchable.

FAN item — potential siblings' baptisms. Patrick was born ~1845 in Ireland; any younger siblings born after the family emigrated to Schuylkill County (~1848) would have been baptized there. A sibling's baptism entry names the father and mother explicitly, supplying the mother's maiden name and directly confirming Thomas as father in a primary original record — unlike the census (indirect) or the death certificate (secondary informant). The Pennsylvania Schuylkill County Church Records are name-searchable; image group 007936751 (Schuylkill County Church Records, 1842-1895) is browse-only (personCount 0) and serves as a fallback for parishes not in the named collection. loc_001 notes that Roman Catholic parishes in Schuylkill County fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia (Archdiocese from 1875), with sacramental registers held at the parish or diocesan level.

FAN item — Thomas Flynn's marriage record. A marriage record for Thomas Flynn would name both spouses, confirm the marital unit, and supply the wife's maiden name — directly addressing the maternal parentage gap. The Pennsylvania Schuylkill County Church Records are name-searchable and cover 1708-1985; image group 007936751 (Church Records, 1842-1895, browse-only (personCount 0)) is the fallback for unindexed parishes. Thomas (born ~1818) and Patrick's birth (~1845 in Ireland) set the marriage window to roughly 1838-1850; a search extended to 1855 captures any remarriage or delayed Pennsylvania church registration. If no Pennsylvania record is found, the marriage likely occurred in Ireland before emigration — a future Irish records search would then be warranted. The mother's maiden name the marriage supplies corroborates Thomas's fatherhood by confirming the couple as a unit, though the marriage alone does not place Patrick with the parents (a separate baptism, census, or probate record is still needed for that link).

Patrick Flynn's own marriage record(s) may name his parents — a common practice in church marriage registers and civil licenses of this period. Patrick's marriage(s) would fall in the documented high-severity timeline gap (1860-1908). The Pennsylvania Schuylkill County Church Records are name-searchable; image group 007936753 (Schuylkill County Marriage Records, 1870-1910) is browse-only (personCount 0) and covers the most probable window. The collection runs past the question's 1908 window; the item is sized to the collection. Note variant spelling Flynn/Flinn in search strategy.

The 1900 census is a gap identified in the proof summary. Patrick would be ~55 and is documented in Schuylkill County through his 1908 death. The 1900 census records immigration year and years in the United States, potentially confirming the Ireland origin and emigration timing visible in earlier censuses. Any children still in Patrick's household might be named for grandparents (a naming-convention lead). The United States Census, 1900 is name-searchable. This item closes the documented timeline from 1860 to the 1908 death certificate.

FAN item — Thomas Flynn's land transactions. Deed records may name Thomas as grantor or grantee, with boundary recitals naming adjoining landowners (frequently neighbors or kin); a deed of gift or conveyance to Patrick specifically would be direct evidence of the parent-child relationship; and post-death sales by heirs would name the children as a group, confirming Patrick's membership in the family. Image group 007936752 (Schuylkill County Deed Records, 1815-1900) is 22% record-searchable, supporting a name search for Thomas Flynn; the remaining images require a browse of the period. Thomas's plausible lifespan (born ~1818) sets the window: 1848 (the family's inferred Pennsylvania arrival from the 1850 census) through ~1895.

- Patrick Flynn (I1): birth ~1845 Ireland (from 1850/1860 census co-evidence); death 12 March 1908 Schuylkill County, PA (death certificate). No ark.
- Thomas Flynn (I2): birth ~1818 Ireland; named as Patrick's father on 1908 death cert (secondary informant: son-in-law James Brown). No ark, no sources.
- 1850 census (S1): Patrick age 5 in Thomas Flynn's Schuylkill County household — indirect (no relationship column); informant indeterminate.
- 1860 census (S2): Patrick age 15 in same household — indirect.
- Both prior census items (pli_004, pli_005) are completed; proof summary ps_001 rates the conclusion "probable," shortfall "gap." Timeline shows a high-severity gap 1860–1908 covering expected marriage, 1870/1880/1900 census, residence. Mother completely unidentified.

**Plan pl_003 — 8 items:**

- **pli_006** | probate | Schuylkill County, PA | 1851–1895 | FamilySearch — Thomas Flynn's will or estate administration; a heir-naming clause is the highest-yield single record remaining. Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 is browse-only (personCount 0); image group 007936749 (Schuylkill probate 1851–1930) likewise browse-only (personCount 0). Thomas's plausible lifespan (born ~1818) sets the window.

- **pli_007** | census | Schuylkill County, PA | 1880 | FamilySearch — Thomas Flynn's household in the first US census with an explicit relationship column; any child still in Thomas's home is labeled "son"/"daughter." Also search Patrick (~35) for grandchild naming patterns. United States Census, 1880 is name-searchable.

- **pli_008** | census | Schuylkill County, PA | 1870 | FamilySearch — Thomas Flynn's household fills the documented 1860–1908 gap; reveals the full sibling set still at home and, critically, names Thomas's wife for the first time — addressing the maternal parentage gap. United States Census, 1870 is name-searchable.

- **pli_009** | church | Schuylkill County, PA | 1848–1875 | FamilySearch — Siblings' baptisms: children of Thomas born after emigration (~1848) would have PA church baptisms naming both father and mother, supplying the mother's maiden name. Pennsylvania Schuylkill County Church Records are name-searchable; image group 007936751 (Schuylkill church records 1842–1895) is browse-only (personCount 0) as fallback.

- **pli_010** | church | Schuylkill County, PA | 1838–1855 | FamilySearch — Thomas Flynn's marriage record names the wife, confirms the couple as a unit, and supplies her maiden name. Pennsylvania Schuylkill County Church Records are name-searchable; image group 007936751 is browse-only (personCount 0) as fallback. If no PA record is found, the marriage likely occurred in Ireland — an Irish records item would follow.

- **pli_011** | vital_record | Schuylkill County, PA | 1865–1905 | FamilySearch — Patrick Flynn's own marriage record(s) may name his parents. Pennsylvania Schuylkill County Church Records name-searchable; image group 007936753 (Schuylkill marriage records 1870–1910) browse-only (personCount 0). Item sized to the collection, not to the 1908 window. Search with both Flynn and Flinn spellings.

- **pli_012** | census | Schuylkill County, PA | 1900 | FamilySearch — Closes the timeline gap; 1900 census records immigration year and years in US, corroborating the Ireland origin. United States Census, 1900 is name-searchable.

- **pli_013** | land | Schuylkill County, PA | 1848–1895 | FamilySearch — Thomas Flynn's deeds; boundary recitals name adjoining owners (frequently kin); a deed of gift to Patrick is direct evidence; post-death heir sales name the children as a group. Image group 007936752 (Schuylkill deeds 1815–1900) is 22% record-searchable; remaining images require a browse. Thomas's lifespan sets the window.

No fallback relationships: each item is independent (the FAN approach spreads across different record types so none depends on another failing first).

8 total searches. The breadth self-check passes: probate, census (three years), church (two functions — siblings and Thomas's marriage), vital/church (Patrick's marriage), land — five distinct record types across all items. At least five items are FAN items (pli_006, pli_007, pli_008, pli_009, pli_010, pli_013 all target Thomas Flynn's or siblings' records rather than Patrick's own).

Hand-back: **search-records** for pli_006 (Thomas Flynn probate browse, FamilySearch), pli_007 (1880 census name search, FamilySearch), pli_008 (1870 census name search, FamilySearch), pli_009 (church records name search, FamilySearch), pli_010 (Thomas marriage name search, FamilySearch), pli_011 (Patrick marriage name search + browse, FamilySearch), pli_012 (1900 census name search, FamilySearch), pli_013 (deed records name search + browse, FamilySearch).

---

The parentage question for Patrick Flynn sits at "probable" because every record found so far places Patrick in Thomas Flynn's household without explicitly stating the relationship — the census columns that would have done so were not introduced until 1880, and the death certificate's informant (a son-in-law) was secondary. The new plan attacks this from multiple FAN directions: first by browsing Thomas Flynn's probate records, where a will naming Patrick as a son would be direct evidence; then by searching the 1880 and 1870 censuses for Thomas's own household, where the 1880 relationship column would state "son" explicitly and the 1870 record would reveal Thomas's wife's name (the mother, still entirely unknown); then by searching for siblings' baptisms in Schuylkill County church records (which name both parents), Thomas's own marriage record (supplying the wife's maiden name), and Patrick's marriage record(s), which sometimes name the groom's parents; then by searching the 1900 census to close the documented timeline gap; and finally by browsing Thomas's deed records for any conveyance naming Patrick as an heir or grantee.

The next step is to begin executing this plan with FamilySearch record searches, starting with the Thomas Flynn probate browse and the 1880 census name search.

- **pli_005** — church, Schuylkill County PA, 1842–1895, FamilySearch — browse-only fallback for pli_004; image group 007936751.

- **pli_007** — other (mine/employment records), Schuylkill County PA, 1878–1900, Pennsylvania State Archives — mine company time books, payroll ledgers, check rolls (Philadelphia and Reading Coal and Iron Company and others), plus Pennsylvania Bureau of Mines annual reports from 1870; most direct evidence for the specific "coal-mining work" claim; Hagley Museum and Library also holds some company records.

This plan addresses whether Michael Sheahan moved to Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania around 1882 to work in the anthracite coal mines. It begins with the 1880 US Federal Census (closest indexed record to the supposed move date, showing both location and occupation), steps back to 1870 to establish a pre-move baseline, and forward to 1900 to test sustained coal-mining residence. After census work, it checks Catholic parish registers (Irish immigrant miners typically appear in church records), then naturalization papers (often stating arrival year and home country), and finally mine company employment records at the Pennsylvania State Archives — the strongest possible direct proof of mining employment.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

entry.rationale: The 1880 US Federal Census (name-searchable, collection 1417683) is the federal enumeration closest to the 1882 arrival claim and captures each person's name, age, birthplace, parents' birthplaces, occupation, and street address. Finding Michael in Schuylkill County in June 1880 would mean he arrived before 1882, refining the tradition; finding him elsewhere in Pennsylvania confirms the move happened after June 1880. His occupation column directly tests the coal-mining claim. The tree's F2 (residence Schuylkill County, 1882) and F3 (occupation Miner, 1882) are both unsourced — this census is the primary verification step. Variant spellings Sheehan, Shahan, and Shehan should also be searched.

The 1870 US Federal Census (name-searchable, collection 1438024) establishes Michael's location and occupation twelve years before the supposed move. The tree's F1 (residence Pennsylvania, 1870) is unsourced and gives only the state, not the county. Finding the county and occupation in 1870 is BCG Standard 11 starting-point verification: if he was already in a coal county in 1870, the 'move around 1882' framing needs reassessment; if he was in a non-mining county or in a non-mining occupation, the later migration to Schuylkill County for mining is a real event to explain. Variant spellings Sheehan, Shahan, and Shehan should be searched.

The 1900 US Federal Census (name-searchable, collection 1325221) records each person's state or country of birth, parents' birthplaces, occupation, years immigrated, years married, and years at current dwelling address. If Michael remained in Schuylkill County through 1900, it shows the coal-mining residency was sustained, not a brief stay. The 'years at current address' column can narrow the arrival date further; the immigration year column (if he was Irish-born) corroborates the migration timeline relative to 1882. Variant spellings Sheehan, Shahan, and Shehan should be searched.

Irish Catholic miners in the anthracite coal region were served by parishes including St. Patrick's (Pottsville) and others. The loc_001 locality entry notes that Roman Catholic sacramental registers were under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875; Diocese of Allentown not erected until 1961) and are held at the parish or diocese. The Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records collection (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) is name-searchable (personCount above 0). A baptism, marriage, or burial entry in a Schuylkill County parish on or after 1882 places Michael in the county through a record independent of the federal census. Variant spellings Sheehan, Shahan, and Shehan should be searched.

Image group 007936751 (Church Records 1842-1895) is browse-only (personCount 0) and covers Catholic and other denomination registers from the coal region not fully captured by the indexed collection. If name searches in the indexed church collection (pli_004) yield nothing, an image browse of this volume may locate records for Michael Sheahan.

Naturalization declarations of intention and petitions for citizenship typically state the applicant's country of birth, date and port of arrival in the United States, and place of residence at filing. If Michael was an Irish immigrant, a document filed in Schuylkill County Court of Common Pleas would confirm his residence in the county and give an approximate US arrival date testable against the 1882 migration claim. It may also state his occupation. Image group 007936750 (Naturalization Records 1849-1915) is browse-only (personCount 0) — image browse required.

Mine company employment records — time books, payroll ledgers, and check rolls — for operators such as the Philadelphia and Reading Coal and Iron Company are held at the Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) and at Hagley Museum and Library. The Pennsylvania Bureau of Mines also published annual reports from 1870 onwards listing colliery statistics and sometimes naming individual miners injured or killed. These records are the most direct evidence for the 'coal-mining work' component of the family tradition: an employment entry showing Michael's hire date, job title (miner vs. laborer vs. door-boy), and colliery name would confirm the specific nature of his work independent of census self-reporting.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

The 1870 US Census is name-searchable on FamilySearch (collection 1438024; personCount above 0). Search for Patrick Flynn in Schuylkill County and separately for Thomas Flynn to locate him whether or not they still share a household.

The 1880 census is the first federal census to record each person's relationship to the head of household explicitly. If Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818, age ~62 in 1880) appears in Patrick's household with the relationship entry 'father,' that is direct evidence of the parent-child relationship and would advance the proof summary conclusion from 'probable' to 'proved.' The 1880 US Census is name-searchable on FamilySearch (collection 1417683; personCount above 0). This is the highest-value item of the three census years because of the explicit relationship column.

If the FamilySearch 1880 search yields no result, Ancestry carries an independently indexed version of the 1880 census that may surface transcription variants of the surname Flynn. Independent indexing has recovered missed entries from the same microfilm rolls when names were rendered differently by different transcribers. The 1880 census is the most valuable of the three years because of its explicit relationship column, so a fallback index is warranted here.

By 1900 Patrick Flynn would be approximately 55. Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818) would be approximately 82 and in all likelihood deceased, but it is worth confirming whether he is still living in Patrick's household — and if he is gone, the 1900 schedule's birthplace-of-father and birthplace-of-mother columns on Patrick's own entry would corroborate his Irish origin. The 1900 US Census is name-searchable on FamilySearch (collection 1325221; personCount above 0). It also records each head's years married, which may add biographical detail useful for other lines of inquiry.

Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818, Ireland) last appears in the 1860 census; Patrick died in 1908. Thomas's death and any will or administration therefore fall somewhere between 1861 and roughly 1905. This window is sized to Thomas's plausible lifespan as creator of the record, not to Patrick's research window. loc_001 identifies the Schuylkill County Register of Wills as a primary parentage source naming heirs, and the Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683-1994 on FamilySearch are browse-only (personCount 0), so this requires an image browse of the county docket volumes rather than a name search. A will naming Patrick as a son would be direct evidence of parentage and would advance the proof summary to 'proved.' This is also the mandatory FAN item for a parentage question: probate files regularly name all heirs and reveal family structure beyond what census records supply.

Independent indexing has recovered missed entries from the same microfilm rolls when names were rendered differently by different transcribers. The 1880 census is the most valuable of the three years because of its explicit relationship column, so a fallback index is warranted here.

By 1900 Patrick Flynn would be approximately 55. Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818) would be approximately 82 and in all likelihood deceased, but it is worth confirming whether he is still living in Patrick's household — and if he is gone, the 1900 schedule's birthplace-of-father and birthplace-of-mother columns on Patrick's own entry would corroborate his Irish origin. Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818, Ireland) last appears in the 1860 census; Patrick died in 1908. Thomas's death and any will or administration therefore fall somewhere between 1861 and roughly 1905. Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

entry.rationale: Patrick Flynn's 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate is already in the project tree as S3, cited on the parentage relationship, but its content has not been formally extracted as research assertions for q_001. Per loc_001, Pennsylvania statewide death registration began in 1906, so a certificate definitely exists for his 12 March 1908 death in Schuylkill County. The informant on a death certificate directly names the decedent's father and mother (and their birthplaces), making this the highest-probability direct parentage evidence available. Formally extract its parentage content.

The 1860 US Census (collection 1473181) is name-searchable with 27 million+ persons. Patrick (~15 in 1860) should still be in Thomas Flynn's household; crucially, the 1860 schedule also names Thomas's wife — the first lead to the mother's identity, which the 1850 census omits. This record is cited as S2 on the parentage relationship in the project tree but its content has not been formally extracted for q_001. Account for Flynn/Flin/Flyn/Flinn spelling variants.

The 1870 US Census (collection 1438024) is name-searchable with 38 million+ persons. Patrick (~25) may have established his own household by 1870; Thomas (~52) and his wife would still appear together if alive. Searching both names would confirm Thomas's continued presence in the county, reveal the wife's name if not found in 1860, and document any siblings still at home. Try Flynn spelling variants.

The 1880 US Census (collection 1417683) is name-searchable with 50 million+ persons and is the first federal census to record each individual's explicit relationship to the head of household. If Patrick (~35) is enumerated as 'son' in Thomas Flynn's household, that relationship column is near-direct parentage evidence. Even if Patrick heads his own household by 1880, Thomas's household would still document the mother and any surviving siblings. Try Flynn spelling variants.

The 1900 US Census (collection 1325221) is name-searchable with 76 million+ persons. Patrick (~55) would head his own household; the 1900 schedule also asks for the birthplace of each person's father and mother, adding a secondary parentage lead. This is the last census in which Patrick can appear, as he died March 1908. Thomas (if alive, ~82) may appear nearby or in Patrick's household.

Thomas Flynn (born ~1818, Ireland) plausibly died between 1860 and 1910; his estate is sized to that lifespan, not to Patrick's research window. A will or estate administration in the Schuylkill County Register of Wills would name his children as heirs, providing direct evidence linking Patrick to Thomas. The Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683–1994 (collection 1999196) is browse-only (personCount 0); Schuylkill County probate image group 007936749 (1851–1930, 412 images) is also 0% name-searchable. This item requires a manual browse of the docket index for 'Flynn.'

The Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records collection (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, 1708–1985) is name-searchable (personCount 982,415). Search for Thomas Flynn and his wife: baptisms of Patrick's younger siblings born in Pennsylvania would name both parents and are direct parentage evidence; burial records for Thomas or his wife may name surviving children. Per loc_001, Roman Catholic parishes in Schuylkill County were under the Diocese of Philadelphia (archdiocese from 1875); sacramental registers are held at the parish and diocesan archives. Try Flynn spelling variants. If the indexed search yields little, the browse-only church records image group 007936751 (1842–1895, 187 images, 0% name-searchable) is a supplemental resource.

A dedicated search for Thomas Flynn's marriage to Patrick's mother is required for this parentage question. The marriage record would confirm Thomas and his wife as a couple, supply the mother's maiden name (only if this was her first marriage — no prior marriage is currently known, but the name should be treated as unverified until further records corroborate it), and by its date relative to Patrick's birth (~1845) would corroborate Thomas as father alongside the census evidence. Note the limit: the couple's marriage proves they wed — it is not by itself evidence that Patrick is their child; that link still needs a record placing Patrick with them. Search the name-searchable SYNTH-PA-CHURCH collection first. If the marriage predates the family's arrival in Pennsylvania or the parish's earliest register, use the browse-only fallback (pli_009).

Fallback for the parents' marriage search (pli_008): browse Schuylkill County church records image group 007936751 (1842–1895, 187 images, browse-only (personCount 0)) manually for Thomas Flynn's marriage entry. Use only when the SYNTH-PA-CHURCH name-searchable collection returns no result for Thomas and wife.

Patrick Flynn's own marriage record would confirm his identity in Schuylkill County, may list his father as bondsman or witness (a common Irish-American practice that provides additional parentage evidence), and establishes his status and community ties before the 1908 death. Search the name-searchable SYNTH-PA-CHURCH collection for a church marriage entry. Also browse the Schuylkill County marriage records image group 007936753 (1870–1910, 94 images, browse-only (personCount 0)) for a civil or civil-recorded church marriage.

The Schuylkill County deed records image group 007936752 (1815–1900, 543 images, 22% name-searchable) may contain land transactions by Thomas Flynn. Land deeds name adjacent landowners and witnesses — FAN evidence placing Thomas in the community and potentially identifying Irish countrymen whose own records can be tracked. A deed naming Patrick as a party (grantee, grantor, or witness) would confirm his continued presence in the county and his association with Thomas. output.text_response:
**Mode: Add-new** — q_001 "Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?"

**Tree facts already recorded that bear on the question:**
- I1 (Patrick Flynn): Birth ~1845, Ireland (sourced by 1850 census); Death 1908-03-12, Schuylkill County, PA (sourced by death certificate). No ark.
- I2 (Thomas Flynn): Birth ~1818, Ireland (unsourced). Linked as Patrick's father by three sources: S1, S2, S3. No mother in the tree.
- 1850 census (S1): Patrick age 5 in Thomas Flynn's Schuylkill County household — indirect evidence of parentage.
- 1860 census (S2): Patrick age 15 in Thomas Flynn's Schuylkill County household — indirect evidence of parentage.
- 1908 death certificate (S3): Names Thomas Flynn as Patrick's father, informant was son-in-law James Brown — direct but secondary evidence.
- Existing proof summary (ps_001): "probable" (not proved); shortfall is a gap — 1870/1880/1900 censuses unsearched, Thomas Flynn's probate unsearched, mother completely unidentified.

---

**Plan pl_003 — 8 items in execution order:**

- **pli_006** — census, Schuylkill County, 1880, FamilySearch — name-searchable. First census with an explicit relationship column; Patrick (~35) or Thomas (~62) in the other's household with a stated "son"/"father" relationship is direct evidence and would advance the proof to proved. ps_001 names this as a primary remaining gap.

- **pli_007** — census, Schuylkill County, 1870, FamilySearch — name-searchable. Thomas (~52) and Patrick (~25) may still share a household; establishes a third consecutive Schuylkill County co-residence and strengthens the corroborating chain before the decisive 1880 search.

- **pli_008** — census, Schuylkill County, 1900, FamilySearch — name-searchable. Patrick (~55) would head his own household; the 1900 schedule records parents' birthplaces, corroborating Ireland as the parents' origin.

- **pli_009** — probate, Schuylkill County, date range 1860–1910, FamilySearch — browse-only. A will naming Patrick as a son is the most likely single record to prove parentage directly. ps_001 names this as the other primary remaining gap.

- **pli_010** — church, Schuylkill County, date range 1835–1850, FamilySearch — name-searchable. Searches for Thomas Flynn's marriage to identify the completely unknown mother; the marriage date also corroborates Thomas as Patrick's father.

- **pli_011** — church, Schuylkill County, date range 1842–1895, FamilySearch — browse-only (**fallback for pli_010**). If the indexed collection returns nothing for Thomas's marriage, browse this film image-by-image.

- **pli_012** — church (FAN), Schuylkill County, date range 1840–1870, FamilySearch — name-searchable. Searches for other children baptized to Thomas Flynn; each sibling's baptism record names both parents, identifying the mother and independently corroborating the parentage.

- **pli_013** — church, Schuylkill County, date range 1865–1890, FamilySearch — name-searchable + browse-only. Patrick's marriage record may name his father, providing an additional independent naming of the Thomas-Patrick relationship.

**Total: 8 searches** (5 name-searchable, 3 browse-only). pli_011 is the only fallback item.

---

The plan picks up where the previous round left off: Thomas Flynn is established as probable father from three sources but the proof is not yet conclusive, and the mother is entirely unknown. The new items work through the three remaining census years in order of evidential weight (1880 first, as the relationship-column census), then Thomas's probate, then four searches targeting the completely unknown mother. The next step is to run search-records against pli_006 (1880 census).

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

Because the birth parish is unlocated, the plan also searches her death/burial record (which routinely states a birthplace in Swedish registers) and reads godparent names on her son's 1718 christening entry, since Swedish godparents were typically family members. Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

Plan written successfully. Here is the return.

**Mode:** Create — first plan for q_001

**Question:** "Where did Josiah Rowe (b. ~1828, Ohio) reside between 1850 and 1865, and with whom was he living?" (q_001)

**Tree facts already recorded (all unsourced):**
- Birth: about 1828, Ohio, United States (F1)
- MilitaryService: 1862-1865, Indiana, United States (F2)
- Death: 1879, Vigo County, Indiana, United States (F3)
- No spouse, parents, or children in the tree

**Plan pl_001 — 8 items in execution order:**

- pli_001 — census / United States / 1850 / FamilySearch — Josiah at ~22 may still be in Ohio or already in Indiana; nationwide name search on "Josiah Rowe" / "Row" / "Roe" answers with whom he was living at the start of the window; census names all household members but not relationships (loc_001 quirk)
- pli_002 — census / Vigo County, Indiana / 1860 / FamilySearch — highest-probability result given his 1879 Vigo County death; collection 1473181 (loc_001); names all cohabitants though not relationships; search on name variants across Indiana
- pli_003 — military / Indiana / 1862-1865 / FamilySearch / NARA — enlistment papers and muster rolls state soldier's residence and next of kin; covers the Civil War portion of the window directly; FamilySearch for index, NARA for full compiled service records
- pli_004 — military / Indiana / 1861-1934 / FamilySearch — collection 1888129 (loc_001); pension or widow's application names marriages, children, and residence across multiple years; especially critical because Indiana had no death registration before 1882 (loc_001 quirk)
- pli_005 — census / Indiana / 1865 / FamilySearch — Indiana state census directly covers the final year of the window, showing post-war household composition
- pli_006 — vital_record / Vigo County, Indiana / 1848-1875 / Vigo County Clerk — not indexed per loc_001 quirk; marriage record names spouse (primary cohabitant) and witnesses/bondsmen (frequently brothers or in-laws); also reveals a married surname affecting earlier name searches
- pli_007 — tax / Vigo County, Indiana / 1848-1866 / Indiana State Archives — annual tax lists fill the inter-census gaps (1851-1859, 1861-1864) and confirm when Josiah arrived in Vigo County from Ohio
- pli_008 — probate / Ohio / 1848-1880 / FamilySearch — FAN item; Josiah's father (born ~1795-1810) likely died in this window; a will naming Josiah identifies his birth family, establishes the Ohio-phase household, and may state his Indiana address; date window set by father's plausible lifespan

**Total scope:** 8 searches across 5 record types, 3 repositories plus county access.

**Hand-back:** search-records for pli_001 through pli_005 (FamilySearch / NARA items); search-external-sites for pli_006 (Vigo County Clerk) and pli_007 (Indiana State Archives); pli_008 is FamilySearch.

---

This plan covers the question of where Josiah Rowe lived between 1850 and 1865, and with whom. It opens with the two federal census years that fall in that window — 1850 (when he may still have been in Ohio with his birth family) and 1860 (when he most likely appears in Vigo County, Indiana, the county where he died in 1879). Both censuses list every person in the household, so finding Josiah in either one directly names his cohabitants. The plan then follows the Civil War thread: his enlistment papers and compiled service record state his residence and next of kin for 1862, and his pension or widow's pension file covers the same years in far greater detail — especially important because Indiana kept no death records before 1882, leaving the pension file as the richest surviving family document. The 1865 Indiana state census closes the window by showing his household right after the war. Three supporting searches round the plan out: a Vigo County marriage record search (to identify his spouse and her family, who would have lived with him), annual county tax lists (to track his presence in the inter-census years), and an Ohio probate search for his father's estate (which may name Josiah as an heir and state his Indiana address, anchoring the 1850 portion of the question). The natural next step is to run the two census name searches on FamilySearch, beginning with the 1860 Vigo County search, which is the most likely to place him directly.
